extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in classical geometry, mechanics, and problem solving (readers/subscribers of The Mathematician, 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of worked problems and short research-style notes in classical Euclidean and analytic geometry and elementary mechanics (moment of inertia, conic sections, collineation), with multiple solution methods and stated propositions. Useful for producing or verifying geometric/analytic solutions and learning standard classical techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remaining shots after removing outer envelope (triangular pile)
rubrics_metrics.description: A little consideration will shew that the number of shot remaining when the outer envelope is removed from the triangular pile is equal to the number that is left when the four bottom strata, or courses, are taken away; and the number remaining when the outer border is removed from a triangular course is equal to the number left when three rows are removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number left is expressed as the triangular summation 1 + 3 + 6 + ... to (n - 4) terms; and writing (n-3) for n will yield the expressions used for subsequent removal of border/courses. Corresponding expressions for square and rectangular piles are given by analogous reductions in n (n diminished by 3 for square pile; m unaffected for rectangular pile) and explicit polynomial formulas are provided in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute moment of inertia of a regular polygon by decomposition into isosceles triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular n-sided polygon consists of n isosceles triangles; the moment of inertia of the polygon about an axis through its centre equals the sum of the moments of inertia of these constituent triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find the moment of each isosceles triangle about required principal axes through its vertex, use coordinate transformations for axes at arbitrary angles, then sum over the n triangles (taking advantage of trigonometric sums over symmetric angular increments which often vanish). Several complete solution methods are given (first, second, third solutions) illustrating this decomposition and summation approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moment of inertia of an isosceles triangle about axes through the vertex (principal axes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let axis a be along the altitude, e the semi-angle at the vertex, a the length of the axis, b the base, A = 1/2 a b the area. Then the moment of inertia about the axis a (through the vertex) and about the perpendicular axis in the plane are given (expressions in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solution shows integration of area elements (lines parallel to the base) and uses similar triangles to express element lengths; explicit integral expressions and final closed forms are supplied. These are then used as building blocks for polygon formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coordinate rotation to obtain moment about an axis making an angle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line through the vertex in the plane makes an angle β with the axis x, the moment about this line can be obtained by transforming co-ordinates: I = I_x cos^2 β + I_y sin^2 β (cross term vanishes for principal axes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put in the known values for I_x and I_y for the isosceles triangle and simplify using trigonometric identities; this yields expressions combining tan e and trig of β that are summed over the polygon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moments of inertia for regular polygon: in-plane vs perpendicular axis relations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a regular polygon the two principal moments about axes in the plane and through the centre are equal (A = B), and the moment about the axis perpendicular to the plane (C) is related to A and the polygon geometry; relations and closed formulas are derived in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry to set A = B and express C in terms of side length and circumradius (or via the triangle decomposition). Then combine with direction cosines of an arbitrary axis making angle a with the plane to obtain the moment about an inclined axis: I = 2A sin^2 a + C cos^2 a, and substitute mass for area × density to give forms in terms of mass M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent solution methods are valid and instructive
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem of polygon moment of inertia is solved by at least three independent methods in the text (direct triangle decomposition with principal axes, integration with element parallel to base, and by using moments A=B=C relations with rectangular axes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each method provides checks on algebra and different insights (symmetry, integration, use of known mechanical results). When producing solutions, present the chosen method clearly and, if possible, relate results to known references (Eameshaw, Walton) as done in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization from plane problems to three-dimensional analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Every plane problem may, in one sense, be regarded as a solid problem by interpreting lines as intersections of planes or curves as intersections of cylinders; analytically, plane problems (combinational form φ(ax+by+1)=0) can be generalized to solid problems V(ax+by+cz+1)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that plane-problem expressions can be embedded in three dimensions (orthographic cylinders, spherical analogies, surfaces converging to a point) and that many plane theorems have analogous 3D counterparts — though explicit performance of generalization can be difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: Two inscribed triangles in a conic circumscribe another conic
rubrics_metrics.description: "If any two triangles be inscribed in a conic section, they will circumscribe another conic section."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by considering tetrahedra inscribed in surfaces of second order and taking limiting processes; the space/surface viewpoint yields an elegant analogical proof which reduces to the planar statement upon intersection with a plane or sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (a) for conic sections through a given parallelogram: common centre
rubrics_metrics.description: All conic sections described through the angular points of a given parallelogram have the same centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By placing axes along adjacent sides AB, AD and using coordinates (AB=m, AD=n) the general circumscribing conic reduces to a central conic with the intersection of diagonals as centre. The algebraic derivation is given (transforming origin to intersection of diagonals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (b) for conic sections: conjugate diameters parallel to sides
rubrics_metrics.description: The diameters of each of these conic sections drawn parallel to the sides of the parallelogram are conjugate diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the reduced central form of the conic and choice of axes; the axes parallel to sides are conjugate diameters for the family of conics through the parallelogram vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (c): tangents at parallelogram vertices form a parallelogram
rubrics_metrics.description: Tangents to each conic at the points A, B, C, D (with axes through the intersection of diagonals) form a parallelogram, and corresponding pairs of tangents intersect on conjugate axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit tangent equations are derived ((6)-(9) in the text) and shown to pairwise be parallel, producing a parallelogram of tangents for each conic in the family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (d): diagonals of circumscribed parallelograms lie on common conjugate diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: The diagonals of the circumscribed parallelograms will lie on common conjugate diameters that are parallel to the sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic coordinate manipulations and symmetry arguments show the diagonals of all such circumscribing parallelograms lie on the same conjugate diameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (e): infinitely many circumscribed parallelograms with diagonals through O
rubrics_metrics.description: About the same parallelogram there can be described an indefinite number of parallelograms the diagonals of which all lie on lines parallel to the sides AB, BC, drawn through the point O (intersection of diagonals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a corollary of the family-of-conics representation (one arbitrary parameter) and the geometric relations derived earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (f): cotangents of angles formed by a diagonal are in arithmetic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: The tangents (or cotangents) of the three angles which one of the diagonals of any parallelogram makes with the other diagonal and the sides are in arithmetical progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is deduced from trigonometric relations arising in the coordinate transformation; angles must be taken on the same side of the diagonal.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3D analogues for parallelopiped: common centre and conjugate diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) All surfaces of the second order described through the angular points of a given parallelopiped have the same centre. (B) The diameters of each drawn parallel to the edges of the parallelopiped are conjugate diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed by placing axes so the eight vertices are coordinate points and derive the reduced central quadric form after translating origin to the common centre; the family again contains one arbitrary parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinear (collineation) systems: definition and mutual correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Two figures (systems of points and lines) are collinear systems if to each point of one system there corresponds a point of the other system such that if three points of the one system are collinear, the three corresponding points are also collinear; hence to each line corresponds a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition is constructive: use sets of corresponding points to induce corresponding lines and intersections; the concept is analogous to pole-polar duality but maps points to points rather than points to lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic form of a collineation between two coordinate systems
rubrics_metrics.description: If (x,y) are coordinates in one system and (t,u) in the corresponding system, the coordinates are related by rational-linear fractional expressions of the form u = (m'y + n'x + p')/(my + nx + l) and t = (m''y + n''x + p'')/(my + nx + l) (equations (3) / reduced to (4) in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given coordinates of four corresponding points one can determine the constants; the mapping is mutual (invertible) and composes transitively (if two systems each collinearly related to a third, they are collinearly related to each other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and role of the collinear centre (coUinear point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each collineation (in general) has a unique collinear point (the coUinear centre) which can be chosen as origin in both systems so that mapping takes the simplified linear-fractional form (equations (4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By translating origins to corresponding points, the mapping simplifies and axes may be chosen so that axis x corresponds to axis t and axis y to axis u. The collinear centre plays the role of fixed canonical point of the mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinear axis: locus where corresponding points coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the collinear centre, all points of a straight line my + nx + l - p = 0 (the 'collinear axis') coincide with their corresponding points in the other system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set x'=x and u'=y in the mapping equations to derive this line; geometrically every line of one system intersects its corresponding line of the other system in a point on the collinear axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter a vis: locus of intersections of images of parallel lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When two parallel lines in one system are mapped, their corresponding lines in the collinear system are generally not parallel; the locus of their intersections is a straight line parallel to the collinear axis called the counter a vis, expressed by my + nx + q = 0 (equation (8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by mapping general parallel line pair equations and finding intersection; this line gives the envelope of intersections corresponding to parallel families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping of axes and special-image lines under collineation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the simplified mapping (with collinear centres placed at origin), the axis of x corresponds to axis of t, axis of y to axis of u, and special lines (like u=0 or t=0) map to explicit linear equations in x,y (see (5)-(6) in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equations (4) to find images of coordinate axes and selected lines; these formulae help construct the correspondence of lines and verify mapping properties.
